headline: High-risk filesystem and shell overlap in ms-swift can create dangerous default interactions; prompt-injection and leakage are lower-confidence due to missing shared-channel evidence.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No shared clipboard, MCP, or browser channel is documented, so direct prompt injection between langchain4j and ms-swift is not evidenced. However, ms-swift reads stdin/stdout and files, and langchain4j can generate text that could be manually bridged into ms-swift. The pathway exists but appears unusual and limited.
conditions: IF an operator copies langchain4j output into ms-swift stdin/stdout or files, injection becomes possible.
IF a shared workspace is introduced, attacker-controlled text can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Avoid copy-pasting model output into ms-swift prompts.
Strip instructions from any text passed between agents.
Use a human review step before forwarding outputs.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: langchain4j reports network_egress:none, while ms-swift has allowlisted egress and handles hub_token/sdk-token plus many file-backed artifacts. There is no documented shared filesystem or common principal, so leakage is not shown by default. The main risk is limited to operator-created sharing of sensitive files or tokens.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in a shared directory accessible to ms-swift, they may be read and uploaded.
IF hub_token or sdk-token are exposed to the pair, ms-swift can transmit associated data to allowlisted services.
mitigations: Store secrets outside shared folders.
Rotate any exposed hub_token or sdk-token.
Use separate OS users for each agent.
Disable access to sensitive directories for ms-swift.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: langchain4j has no write or shell capabilities documented, but ms-swift can execute shell, spawn subprocesses, install packages, and write the filesystem. If both are pointed at the same directory or project, ms-swift can overwrite artifacts that langchain4j consumes or produces. Uncertainty about shared state pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same writable directory, ms-swift can clobber files used by langchain4j.
IF the orchestrator lacks locking, concurrent writes can race on shared artifacts.
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories.
Run ms-swift under a separate OS account.
Disable package installation unless needed.
Add file locks around shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: implement workspace locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: langchain4j can generate assistant text, and ms-swift can consume stdin/stdout and files, so A's output can become B's input. There is no documented verification gate in ms-swift, and no evidence that langchain4j marks outputs as untrusted. This creates a plausible default cascade from generated text into downstream actions, though not proven to be fully automated.
conditions: IF langchain4j output is piped into ms-swift without validation, errors can cascade.
IF ms-swift uses generated text to drive shell or training commands, bad instructions can propagate.
mitigations: Insert a validation step between agents.
Require schema checks on all handoffs.
Log and review any shell commands generated by ms-swift.
Use allowlists for downstream actions.
requires-engineering: add typed contracts between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source customer-support tools, but ms-swift explicitly handles hub_token/sdk-token and many data classes including datasets, checkpoints, and evaluation outputs. langchain4j has no documented sensitive-data handling or residency controls. The mismatch is mainly around retention and secret handling, so medium fits better than low given the broader data surface.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed through ms-swift, its token and artifact handling must satisfy the applicable policy.
IF retention requirements differ between the two deployments, stored outputs may violate policy.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in ms-swift artifacts.
Keep tokens in a secret manager.
Set short log retention.
Review data handling docs before deployment.
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls.
